ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: There are seven circles in the figure. At the top there are three circles arranged in a horizontal straight line and connected by line segments; in the middle there are also three circles arranged in a horizontal straight line and connected by line segments; the middle circle of the top row, the center circle of the middle row, and the circle below with a question mark written in it are again on the same vertical line and connected by line segments. Reasoning: According to the method, mark the top row as A-B-C, the middle row as D-E-F, the lower question-mark circle as X, and the vertical line as B-E-X. The problem requires that the products of the three numbers on the three straight lines be the same, so A·B·C = D·E·F = B·E·X. The seven numbers are all different, and according to the method take nonzero single digit positive integers. From A·B·C = B·E·X, B can be canceled, giving A·C = E·X; from D·E·F = B·E·X, E can be canceled, giving D·F = B·X. Therefore, for a given X, the two center numbers B and E each must make X·y able to be decomposed into the product of two other unused and different single digit numbers. Check X=1 to 9: when X=1, there are only 6→2·3 and 8→2·4, and it is impossible to assign two non-conflicting factor pairs to the two center numbers; when X=2, there can be 3→1·6, 4→1·8, 6→3·4, 9→3·6, among which center numbers 4 and 9 can be taken, with factor pairs respectively 1·8 and 3·6, not conflicting with each other; when X=3, the possible factor pairs are 2→1·6, 4→2·6, 6→2·9, 8→4·6, but choosing any two will overlap or use another center number; when X=4, the possibilities are 2→1·8, 3→2·6, 6→3·8, also not compatible; X=5 and 7 have not enough usable decompositions; when X=6, the possibilities are 1→2·3, 2→3·4, 3→2·9, 4→3·8, not compatible; when X=8, there are only 1→2·4 and 3→4·6, overlapping; when X=9, there is only 2→3·6, not enough for two center numbers. Therefore the only feasible one is X=2. A concrete construction is: let B=9, E=4, X=2, take A,C as 1,8, and take D,F as 3,6, then 1·9·8 = 3·4·6 = 9·4·2 = 72.

method.method_draft: First describe the diagram: there are seven circles arranged as a top horizontal line of three circles, a middle horizontal line of three circles, and a vertical line through the top-middle circle, the center circle, and the bottom circle marked with '?'. Label the top row A-B-C, the middle row D-E-F, and the bottom question-mark circle X, with the vertical line B-E-X. From the text, the products on A-B-C, D-E-F, and B-E-X are equal, and all seven entries are distinct single-digit positive digits. Write AB C = DE F = BE X. Since digits are nonzero, cancel B in ABC = BEX to get AC = EX, and cancel E in DEF = BEX to get DF = BX. Now test possible X from 1 to 9: for each candidate X, find which possible central digit y allows Xy to be factored as a product of two other distinct unused single digits. A valid X must allow two compatible central digits B and E with disjoint factor pairs. This factor-pair check leaves only X = 2: take central digits 9 and 4, with 4·2 = 8 = 1·8 and 9·2 = 18 = 3·6, giving common product 72. Therefore the question-mark circle is 2.
